stories.headline: All Support Acts Quit Ed Sheeran's US Tour After Macklemore Dropped Over Pro-Palestinian Remarks
stories.summary:
All remaining support acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour have withdrawn after rapper Macklemore was dropped from the lineup for making pro-Palestinian statements during two concerts in New Jersey earlier this month. Macklemore displayed images of devastation in Gaza and called for a "free Palestine," prompting criticism from Jewish groups and pressure on promoters Messina Touring Group to remove him. Finneas, brother of Billie Eilish, Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham, and Irish folk band Beoga — who perform with Sheeran nightly — all announced their departures within hours of each other.

Sheeran issued a statement distancing himself from the promoter's decision, saying he had attempted to broker a resolution with venues but was ultimately not responsible for Macklemore's removal. He described himself as "appalled" by the Israel-Gaza conflict and acknowledged having personal views, but explained he intentionally keeps politics off his professional platform, citing his young and diverse audience. "I am not complicit," he wrote, adding that there is "room for multiple approaches" to advocating for peace.

The departing artists framed their exits as a matter of principle. Lukas Graham said artists "must be able to speak about war" and "about children" caught in conflict. Finneas stated that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." The episode reflects a broader tension in the entertainment industry over where performers stand on the Gaza conflict and whether promoters and venues can or should police political speech.

The walkout leaves Sheeran's ongoing US tour without a full supporting lineup and has reignited public debate about free speech, political expression at concerts, and the obligations of major artists to take public stances on geopolitical conflicts. The story has drawn coverage from six outlets spanning the political spectrum.

stories.headline: News Helicopter Crashes in Fireball Near Deadly LA Bus Wreck, Killing at Least One
stories.summary:
A news helicopter crashed and erupted in flames near Chatsworth in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening, killing at least one person — believed to be a pedestrian not aboard the aircraft — as emergency crews were already on scene responding to a separate, deadly Metro bus collision nearby. The Los Angeles Fire Department said firefighters were still searching the wreckage to determine how many people were on board. Early reports indicated the helicopter belonged to NBC affiliate KNBC.

The bus crash, reported shortly after 5 p.m. near Nordhoff Street and De Soto Avenue, killed at least two people and injured six others who were transported to hospitals. The helicopter came down between two commercial buildings on the 9100 block of Mason Avenue, setting several nearby cars ablaze. Firefighters extinguished the fires but remained on scene.

KNBC anchor Colleen Williams broke down on air while covering the story, saying the station had "lost contact" with crew members. The National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the helicopter crash. The convergence of two fatal incidents at the same location underscored the scale of the emergency response required.

stories.headline: Mount Etna Ash Cloud Grounds All Flights at Sicily's Catania Airport Through Tuesday Evening
stories.summary:
All arrivals and departures at Catania International Airport in Sicily have been suspended through at least 22:00 local time Tuesday due to a fresh ash cloud from Mount Etna, Italy's tallest active volcano. The INGV Etneo Observatory issued a red aviation alert — the highest level — on Monday as ongoing volcanic activity intensified. Airport officials advised passengers to check with their airlines before traveling to the terminal.

The closure marks the second major disruption at Catania in recent months. The airport, Italy's fifth busiest by passenger traffic and handling roughly 12 million passengers per year, was shut for nearly a week during the peak summer season last month due to Etna's activity. Etna, standing at 3,324 meters and located approximately 40 kilometers from the airport, erupts frequently and has long posed a logistical challenge for Sicilian aviation.

The repeated disruptions have intensified calls from aviation experts and travel groups to consider relocating or expanding airport infrastructure elsewhere in Sicily. Despite the hazards, Etna's eruptions attract significant tourism, with approximately 1.5 million visitors to the volcano each year and large crowds drawn to last month's visible lava flows.

stories.headline: Cleveland City Council Votes to Rename Portion of Lake Erie the 'Gulf of Cleveland' in Jab at Trump
stories.summary:
The Cleveland, Ohio, City Council voted 13-1 on Monday to rename a portion of Lake Erie the "Gulf of Cleveland," a symbolic rebuke aimed at President Trump's executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The emergency resolution was led by Councilmember Kris Harsh and mirrors Trump's earlier move to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America."

The vote carries no binding geographic or federal authority but was intended as a pointed political statement from a major American city on the shores of the Great Lakes. It reflects ongoing friction between municipal governments and the Trump administration over executive naming powers and federal overreach into geography that many Midwesterners view as culturally significant.

The move drew coverage from two outlets and highlights a pattern of local governments using symbolic legislative actions to push back against Trump administration policies. No legal challenge has been announced in connection with the Cleveland resolution.

stories.headline: Pentagon Inspector General Confirms U.S. Munitions Shortfalls From Iran War, Contradicting Trump
stories.summary:
The Defense Department's inspector general has confirmed that the U.S. war with Iran has produced significant munitions shortfalls, directly contradicting President Trump's repeated public claims that American weapons stockpiles are "virtually unlimited." The independent watchdog found the U.S. spent more than $22 billion on munitions between February and June, resulting in "strategic inventory shortfalls" and industrial base bottlenecks for resupply. The report also disclosed $3.7 billion in equipment losses, including four F-15E fighter jets, one F-35 Joint Strike Fighter, and 30 MQ-9 drones, with total U.S. war expenditures reaching $33.4 billion over that period.

A separate Congressional Budget Office estimate released the same day put the total cost of the conflict even higher, at $38 billion when accounting for replaced munitions, equipment losses, increased flight hours, and higher fuel costs. Previous independent estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies had found stocks of Patriot missiles and THAAD interceptors depleted by more than half in some cases.

The White House rejected the inspector general's findings, with spokeswoman Anna Kelly stating the military has "more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had previously called news reporting on shortages "not true," and Trump described such reporting as "treasonous."

The report is significant because it represents a rare independent, public glimpse into typically classified weapons stockpile data, and its findings conflict sharply with official administration characterizations of the war's toll on U.S. military readiness. The munitions bottleneck raises questions about American capacity to respond to additional security contingencies while the Iran conflict continues.

stories.headline: Nigeria Arrests Alleged Mexican Drug Kingpin, Uncovers Third Industrial Meth Lab in Four Months
stories.summary:
Nigerian authorities have arrested an alleged Mexican drug cartel figure at Lagos's international airport and uncovered what they describe as an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the third such discovery linked to Mexican nationals in the country in four months. Arturo Carrera Loaiza, 40, was detained after officials found digital images on his phone showing him in a laboratory coat alongside equipment consistent with meth production. Location data embedded in those images led investigators to a property in Ebonyi state containing chemicals and drug-making equipment.

A CCTV memory card recovered at the suspected lab showed footage of a person resembling Loaiza directing others as they removed chemicals and equipment from the site. A separate raid in Oyo state in June and another discovery a month prior involved additional Mexican nationals and Nigerian co-conspirators at similarly concealed facilities in forests and rural areas. Loaiza has denied any involvement, claiming he was in Nigeria for a restaurant business venture.

Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency chairman, Gen. Mohamed Buba Marwa, said the pattern of discoveries indicates that international criminal organizations are attempting to establish drug production infrastructure inside Nigeria's forests and rural communities. Unlike plant-based narcotics, synthetic drugs such as methamphetamine can be manufactured anywhere with the necessary chemicals and expertise, making Nigeria's rural areas attractive to cartels seeking to relocate from jurisdictions with stronger enforcement.

The findings signal an emerging and potentially significant shift in global narco-trafficking patterns, with West Africa increasingly targeted as a production hub by Mexican drug syndicates. Investigations into the financing and facilitation networks behind the Nigerian operations are ongoing.

stories.headline: Emmy Awards: Welsh Actor Matthew Rhys Makes History With Double Lead Acting Win
stories.summary:
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys became the first person in Emmy Awards history to win two lead acting prizes in a single night, taking home honors for his roles in the supernatural comedy "Widow's Bay" and the psychological thriller "The Beast In Me." No actor had previously achieved the double win, though a small number including Alan Alda, Sally Field, and Elisabeth Moss had previously been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year.

Rhys won best lead actor in a limited series for "The Beast In Me," in which he co-starred with Claire Danes, and best lead actor in a comedy for his portrayal of a mayor in "Widow's Bay." On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award to "the great and good people of Wales," calling his nation "small but mighty."

Other notable winners included Jean Smart, who claimed her fifth Emmy for the final season of "Hacks" and her eighth career acting Emmy overall, tying the all-time record for most acting wins. Allison Janney also won her eighth Emmy for "The Diplomat," equaling the same record. Stephen Colbert and Kate O'Flynn were among additional winners, and the ceremony featured an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a humanitarian award for Michael J. Fox.

stories.headline: Japan's Centenarian Population Exceeds 100,000 for First Time as Demographic Crisis Deepens
stories.summary:
Japan's health ministry has reported that the number of people aged 100 or older in the country has surpassed 100,000 for the first time, reaching 107,677 — the highest centenarian count of any nation in the world. Women account for 88 percent of the total. The milestone was announced ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government sends personal letters and traditional sake cups to those turning 100.

Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno credited advances in medicine and technology, as well as Japan's diet — heavy in fish, vegetables, and rice and low in saturated fat — and an active lifestyle among older residents. However, he warned of mounting pressure on the country's social security system as the elderly population grows while the overall population shrinks.

The centenarian milestone arrives against a backdrop of deepening demographic strain. Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14 last year, well below the 2.1 replacement level, and Prime Minister Sanae Takichi has described the population decline as a "quiet emergency." The country's total population is projected to fall from a 2008 peak of 128 million to approximately 87 million by 2070, with residents 65 and older expected to comprise nearly 40 percent of the population by that year.

Government programs and subsidies aimed at encouraging higher birth rates have not produced measurable results. Immigration remains limited, with foreigners making up only about 3 percent of the population and public opposition to expansion growing. Japan's demographic trajectory is watched closely by other aging nations facing similar pressures on pension and healthcare systems.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Dismisses AI Safety as 'Hoax' as Congress Faces Deadlock on Regulation
stories.summary:
President Trump on Monday declared on social media that AI 'taking over the World, destroying Humanity' is a 'HOAX,' asserting that the only guardrails AI needs are a 'strong and smart' president. His remarks came as Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark warned that a major AI accident could trigger sweeping restrictions that would ultimately hurt U.S. competition with China, telling Fox News that 'the worst time to react to an exponential is when it's too late.'

The political deadlock on Capitol Hill has made new AI safety legislation a remote prospect in the near term. The House is set to enter recess at the end of this week ahead of November midterm elections, and Speaker Mike Johnson gave no indication he would delay that schedule, calling the issue 'very complex.' Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries urged Congress not to leave town until action is taken, and a bipartisan letter from House members called the imperative to act beyond dispute.

Republicans, aligned with Trump's opposition to new regulations, are unlikely to advance legislation that would require his signature to take effect. Some Democrats and at least one Republican, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, have called for a special session, though that outcome is considered highly unlikely. Trump is expected to convene a White House meeting with AI executives to discuss corporate responsibility.

The debate reflects a sharp partisan divide: conservatives largely back Trump's position that heavy regulation would cede ground to China and stifle innovation, while Democrats and several prominent AI researchers argue that without binding safety standards the U.S. is exposed to catastrophic and irreversible risk. Former Vice President Kamala Harris separately called for a treaty with China to slow AI development and adopt global testing standards.

stories.headline: FBI Director Patel Defends Lowering Hiring Standards on Bestiality and Prostitution Before Senate
stories.summary:
FBI Director Kash Patel appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday in his first public testimony since the bureau's revised hiring standards were reported in August, defending the removal of automatic disqualifications for applicants with histories involving bestiality, prostitution, and employment theft. Patel argued the changes were intended to protect victims of trafficking and sexual abuse who would otherwise be barred from federal law enforcement careers.

'We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked,' Patel told Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin, insisting that candidates still face the same rigorous application process. Under the new standards, applicants who engaged in acts of bestiality before the age of 18 may still be considered; those with prostitution histories are eligible if the conduct occurred more than 10 years ago and involved fewer than three incidents; and employment theft is permissible if it occurred more than three years prior.

Lawmakers from both parties expressed skepticism and pressed Patel repeatedly over the changes, with Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana among those who questioned the bureau's reasoning. Critics note that the revised standards do not distinguish between those coerced into sexual conduct with animals and those who participated willingly, a point that drew pointed questioning during the hearing.

Democrats on the committee sent a letter to Patel on the eve of the hearing demanding a full accounting and data on how many applicants have been hired or extended conditional offers under the new eligibility criteria since they took effect on June 16. The hearing marks the first official congressional oversight of the changes.

stories.headline: House Democrats Split Over Russia Sanctions Bill as Vote Looms This Week
stories.summary:
House Democratic leadership is opposing a Russia sanctions bill named in honor of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that is set for a vote this week, but rank-and-file members are not fully aligned with that stance. Republicans are expected to need some Democratic votes to offset defections from their isolationist wing, making the minority party's position pivotal to the bill's fate.

At the center of Democratic objections is a provision that would allow the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on targeted countries — a mechanism that critics say hands the executive branch sweeping unilateral economic power. Some Democrats are wary of being seen as opposing measures to hold Russia accountable, while leadership argues the tariff authority is too broad a concession to a president they distrust.

The bill's outcome could have significant consequences for U.S. policy toward Russia at a moment when the war in Ukraine and related energy-price pressures remain dominant concerns. Whether the measure passes will depend on how many Democrats break with leadership and how many Republican isolationists ultimately vote against their own party's bill.

The vote comes as Congress also faces pressure to address AI regulation and other issues before its scheduled recess at the end of the week, compressing the legislative calendar and raising the stakes on whichever priorities leadership chooses to advance.

stories.headline: U.S. Median Household Income Hits 58-Year High as Poverty Rate Declines, Census Bureau Reports
stories.summary:
The U.S. Census Bureau's annual income and poverty report released Tuesday shows that the median American household earned $87,460 in 2025, breaking a record that had stood for 58 years and representing a significant gain over the prior year. The official poverty rate also declined, and health insurance coverage remained largely unchanged from 2024.

The report offers a broad measure of economic well-being across the country, though analysts note that gains were not uniform across all demographic groups. The data covers 2025 and reflects conditions before the most recent rounds of tariff-driven price increases and energy market disruptions began to affect household budgets in 2026.

The findings are likely to become a flashpoint in ongoing debates over economic policy, with supporters of the administration pointing to the record income figure as evidence of underlying economic strength and critics arguing that subsequent inflation and energy costs have since eroded real purchasing power for many families.

The Census Bureau's annual report is one of the most closely watched indicators of whether economic growth is translating into tangible improvements for ordinary Americans, and the data will inform both the policy debate and political messaging ahead of the November midterm elections.

stories.headline: Update: Satellite Images Show Major Damage to Saudi Oil Pipeline as Brent Crude Surges Past $108
stories.summary:
New satellite imagery analyzed by BBC Verify reveals severe damage to a pumping station along Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline following a strike attributed to Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, with experts now estimating repairs could take four to six weeks. The closure of the pipeline — a critical export route increasingly used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing Iran-U.S. conflict — could reduce global oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day, or roughly 3.6 percent of world demand. Brent crude reached $108 a barrel on Tuesday.

The Saudi government said Tuesday it would respond 'firmly' to attacks by Yemen's Houthi group, which has also expanded its territorial control along the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, strengthening its ability to enforce a declared blockade of Saudi shipping. Separate satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base, where U.S.-made F-15 fighter jets are stationed, following Houthi missile and drone strikes.

Energy analysts warn the compounding disruptions — pipeline closure, Houthi territorial gains along key waterways, and ongoing attacks on Saudi infrastructure — represent a serious structural threat to global oil supply chains. Anne-Sophie Corbeau of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy said the strikes illustrate that pipeline workarounds to avoid the Strait of Hormuz 'may not be super useful because they can be destroyed.'

The escalation marks a significant widening of the conflict in the Arabian Peninsula. The Houthis, backed by Iran, have now seized control of significant territory across Yemen's southwestern coast, including areas overlooking Bab al-Mandab, a chokepoint through which a substantial share of global seaborne oil trade passes. Saudi Arabia has retaliated with strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.

stories.headline: Update: What Weapon Has the U.S. Deployed in Space? Analysts Weigh Options
stories.summary:
Following the U.S. government's confirmation that it has deployed the first-ever space weapon in Earth's orbit, defense analysts are publicly speculating about the weapon's nature and capabilities. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink described it only as necessary to safeguard U.S. forces against hostile enemy action, offering no details on its design, capabilities, or the date it was placed in orbit.

Experts consulted by the BBC said the most likely candidate is an electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform capable of disrupting satellite communications — a non-destructive but operationally significant capability. Less likely but possible options include a kinetic kill vehicle or a close-inspection and grappling satellite capable of physically manipulating or destroying adversary satellites.

The announcement arrives amid an intensifying space arms race. Russia and China have in recent years conducted extensive 'rendezvous and proximity operations,' maneuvering their own satellites close to Western assets in what analysts describe as potential rehearsals for hunter-killer tactics. China has also demonstrated 'space tug capability,' the ability to grapple and reposition satellites in orbit.

The U.S. deployment signals a new phase in great-power competition beyond Earth's atmosphere, formalizing what had previously been an unofficial threshold. Experts say the move is likely to accelerate similar developments by Russia and China, raising concerns about the long-term stability of the orbital environment and the risk of debris-generating conflicts in space.

stories.headline: Canada Pitches Itself as 'Safe Harbour' for Global Investment as New U.S. Tariffs Take Effect
stories.summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives in Toronto on Tuesday, pitching Canada as a 'safe harbour' for international capital amid geopolitical and trade uncertainty. The summit participants collectively represent more than C$120 trillion in assets, and Ottawa is seeking commitments across sectors including defense, energy, mining, artificial intelligence, and infrastructure.

The summit coincided with the entry into force of new U.S. tariffs on a range of Canadian goods — a direct consequence of the collapse of trade talks between Ottawa and Washington last month. Carney announced plans to privatize operations at four of Canada's largest airports, a move intended to raise billions of dollars for reinvestment in transport infrastructure. He addressed American executives in the room directly, framing Canada as a stable alternative destination for capital.

Carney's government has been actively diversifying economic partnerships with Europe, Asia, and the Middle East following the deterioration of the U.S.-Canada trade relationship. High-profile attendees included Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, and Blackstone president Jon Gray. The prime minister's office cautioned against expecting major announcements, describing the event primarily as an opportunity for investors to assess Canada's business environment.

Economic analysts have noted that Canada faces real structural hurdles in attracting investment, including an uncompetitive tax and regulatory environment and skilled-labor shortages. The summit is seen as a test of whether Carney — a former central banker with deep ties in global finance — can translate those relationships into tangible economic commitments at a moment of acute trade pressure.

stories.headline: Flash Flooding Strikes New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut, Prompting Water Rescues
stories.summary:
Severe flash flooding struck the tri-state area of New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut on Tuesday, submerging vehicles, prompting water rescues, and disrupting a regional half-marathon whose participants were seen wading through waist-deep floodwaters. Connecticut officials reported that parts of the state received up to seven inches of rain in a very short period of time.

Emergency responders conducted multiple rescues of stranded motorists across affected areas. The storm represents one of the more significant acute weather events to hit the densely populated northeastern corridor in recent months, though no fatalities had been confirmed in initial reports.

The flooding underscores the increasing frequency of extreme precipitation events in the northeastern United States, a pattern climate scientists have linked to rising atmospheric moisture content associated with warming temperatures. The affected region is home to tens of millions of residents.

stories.headline: NATO Shoots Down Drone Over Lithuania as Russia Fires Flares at Danish Helicopter
stories.summary:
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, likely crossing from neighboring Belarus shortly after midnight Tuesday. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda confirmed the intercept, calling it a demonstration of NATO readiness amid intensifying Russian aggression against Ukraine. It is believed to be the first time a NATO jet has destroyed a drone in Lithuanian airspace; drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region.

On the same day, Denmark accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its military helicopters during a routine photographic operation in the Baltic Sea. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the incident 'reckless' and said it was designed to 'intimidate and divide.' Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador; European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called Russia's behavior part of 'a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe.'

Russia said it would 'thoroughly investigate' the Baltic Sea incident but accused Danish helicopters of making 'dangerous manoeuvres' near its warships. Moscow has not commented on the Lithuanian drone incident. The debris from the downed drone will be examined to determine origin, whether it was armed, and whether the incursion was deliberate.

The twin incidents mark a significant escalation in military tensions along NATO's eastern flank, coming as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues. Lithuania shares a large portion of its border with Belarus, a key Russian ally, and has seen a series of drone incursions in recent months.

stories.headline: Trump Jr. and Wife Confirm Putin Ally Paid Hundreds of Thousands for Wedding Festivities
stories.summary:
Donald Trump Jr. and his wife Bettina Trump confirmed Monday that two nights of their three-day May wedding celebration on a private Bahamian island were partially funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to President Vladimir Putin. The acknowledgment came after ProPublica published an investigation detailing that Kremlev paid 'hundreds of thousands of dollars' for the festivities, including a roughly $70,000 fireworks display and island rental fees of approximately $100,000 per night.

The couple said in an Instagram statement that Kremlev, a 'dear friend,' hosted 'two incredible nights of celebrations' as 'an extraordinarily generous wedding gift.' A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told ProPublica that the two men have a personal friendship and no business relationship. Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association, an organization funded by state-backed Gazprom energy company; he has also received Russia's Order of Friendship and traveled in Putin's delegation to China earlier this year.

Because Donald Trump Jr. is a private citizen and not a U.S. government employee, accepting gifts from a foreign national is not illegal. However, ethics watchdog groups raised concerns about the appearance of a conflict of interest. Jordan Libowitz of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington said: 'People don't just give hundreds of thousands of dollars to a random acquaintance without wanting something.'

Other wedding attendees included Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, who has played a diplomatic role in U.S. negotiations with Russia, Iran, and in the Middle East. The story is drawing broad coverage across the political spectrum, with critics arguing it raises questions about foreign influence proximity to the White House and defenders noting the legal distinction between a private citizen and a government official.

stories.headline: Kennedy Center Faces Imminent Bankruptcy, Board May Vote to Close Building Tuesday
stories.summary:
The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., is on the brink of bankruptcy and could close as soon as Tuesday, according to a report by The Washington Post. The institution's board of trustees — chaired by President Donald Trump — has been presented with a 57-page internal report warning of 'certain fiscal collapse,' with the center unable to pay employees or meet maintenance costs within weeks.

The board is expected to meet Tuesday to consider two pressing issues: the financial crisis and deteriorating physical condition of the building. Trustees are reportedly recommending the main building be closed immediately due to costs. The report also suggests that attaching Trump's name to the facade may be the only way to attract the donor support necessary to stave off collapse.

The center was projected to collect only about $124 million of a budgeted $220 million in revenue this past fiscal year, leaving a roughly $23 million deficit even after spending cuts. A center spokesperson attributed the problems to 'financial mismanagement by previous leadership' and said Trump's involvement had attracted new donors. Critics, however, point to an exodus of artists and audience members following Trump's self-installation as chairman in 2025 and a subsequent attempt — later blocked in court — to rename the venue the 'Trump-Kennedy Center.'

Ticket sales fell to their lowest levels since the COVID-19 pandemic after Trump assumed the chairmanship, with numerous artists canceling performances in protest. The episode reflects ongoing tensions over the administration's approach to federally supported cultural institutions.

stories.headline: Pennsylvania Man Arrested With Rifle and Ammunition After Allegedly Pledging Allegiance to ISIS
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors announced Tuesday that a 21-year-old Pennsylvania man, Jonathan Hunter Kramer of Valencia, was arrested after FBI agents tracked him to a hotel and seized a semiautomatic rifle, five magazines, and 190 rounds of ammunition. Kramer had allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS online, offered to distribute explosives manuals, and written about preparing for his 'mission' while using the alias 'Hamza Al Rashid.'

Kramer is charged with receiving a firearm and ammunition knowing they would be used to commit a federal crime of terrorism, including providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization. Investigators say an anonymous tip in March — shortly after his release from a juvenile detention facility — restarted a federal inquiry first opened in 2023, when Kramer was charged as a minor in connection with a separate mass-casualty plot and for possessing child sexual abuse material.

FBI agents observed Kramer buy a disposable phone, accept a long black bag from another person in a parking lot, and check into a hotel in Cranberry Township paying cash before traveling to a sporting goods store's gun counter. A search of Kramer, the hotel room, and his home also turned up a rifle scope and bipod, about 30 knives, pepper spray, and a handwritten note. No attack had been carried out at the time of the arrest.

The case follows a series of ISIS-related domestic terrorism arrests in recent months and underscores ongoing FBI efforts to monitor individuals with prior juvenile terrorism adjudications after their release from custody.

stories.headline: U.S. Confirms First-Ever Deployment of Space Weapon in Earth's Orbit
stories.summary:
The United States has publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has deployed a weapon in Earth's orbit, marking a historic admission of offensive military capabilities in space. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink made the disclosure at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, saying the weapon was necessary to safeguard U.S. forces against hostile enemy action. He did not elaborate on the weapon's type, specific capabilities, or when it was placed in orbit.

Military experts say the weapon could range from an electronic warfare or radio jamming platform to a kinetic kill vehicle capable of destroying enemy satellites, though analysts caution that publicly available information remains extremely limited. A U.S. Space Force spokesperson confirmed the service employs both kinetic and non-kinetic means to 'disrupt, degrade, and even destroy' adversary capabilities in space. The acknowledgment comes as the Trump administration advances its 'Golden Dome' missile defense initiative, which includes space-based interceptors.

China responded swiftly on Tuesday, with a foreign ministry spokesman warning against an 'arms race' in space and urging the U.S. to 'stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space.' The disclosure underscores an accelerating militarization of space driven by rival Russian and Chinese programs targeting U.S. satellites. A 1967 treaty bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit but does not prohibit other categories of space weapons.

stories.headline: China Imposes Sweeping New Travel Restrictions on Citizens, Including Tech Workers
stories.summary:
China has enacted broad new regulations restricting the ability of its citizens to travel abroad, granting authorities expanded powers to bar individuals deemed a threat to national security, industrial interests, or technological security. Citizens found to have 'harmed' China's national security or interests while overseas can be barred from leaving the country for up to three years under the new rules. Border officials are also now required to advise citizens against traveling to countries designated as 'high-risk.'

The rules have significant implications for workers in sensitive technology sectors, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence — industries at the center of the U.S.-China rivalry. Earlier this year, co-founders of AI company Manus were reportedly barred from leaving China after it was acquired by Meta. Civil servants and state-owned enterprise employees have already been subject to informal passport controls for years, with some required to surrender passports to employers.

Western legal scholars and human rights observers described the move as a significant escalation of ideological control under President Xi Jinping, with one Georgetown University professor likening it to restrictions seen under Mao Zedong's era, when China was largely cut off from the world. The Chinese government has framed some of the measures as aimed at preventing corrupt officials from fleeing or transferring assets abroad, though critics say the scope extends far beyond that justification.

stories.headline: Suspected Sabotage Causes Widespread Rail Disruption Across Netherlands
stories.summary:
Major rail disruptions swept across the Netherlands on Tuesday after the country's railway operator ProRail reported what it described as suspected deliberate sabotage to the national rail network. Materials, including metal pipes approximately 1.5 meters in length, were found placed on tracks at multiple locations, causing widespread signal and crossing failures. ProRail confirmed the disruption appeared to be 'an intentional disruption caused by human action,' and the national police unit launched an investigation.

At least 15 separate disruptions were recorded across the country, affecting routes to Schiphol international airport, Utrecht, and several other major destinations in the center and north of the Netherlands. No suspects or motives have been identified as of Tuesday. The incident follows a recent French investigation into whether a separate train derailment in France was also caused by a malicious act.

The sabotage highlights growing concerns across Europe about the vulnerability of critical transportation infrastructure to deliberate attack. The Netherlands is a major European transit hub, and disruption to its rail network affects both domestic commuters and international passengers. Investigations are ongoing.

stories.headline: Anthrax Outbreak Kills Dozens of Animals in Zambia, Infects 12 People
stories.summary:
Zambian authorities have issued urgent public warnings after an anthrax outbreak killed dozens of wild animals — including 46 hippos, eight elephants, five buffalo, and a crocodile — in the Munyamadzi Game Management Area in Muchinga province since July. Twelve people have been infected with anthrax after consuming meat from dead wildlife in the affected area, officials said over the weekend. No human deaths have been reported, and the infected individuals are receiving treatment.

Zambia's Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit said local communities in the affected region depend on wildlife for food, and that carcasses from the outbreak were consumed before the danger was recognized. Authorities have called for a suspension of hunting in the area and urged the public not to consume, sell, distribute, or handle meat from animals that die suddenly or from suspected anthrax infection. Laboratory investigations and surveillance are ongoing to determine the full geographic extent of the outbreak.

Anthrax is endemic to Zambia but large-scale human infections are uncommon. The country experienced a severe outbreak in 2023, which killed four people and spread across nine of ten provinces. The disease is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, whose spores can persist in soil for years and enter animals through inhalation or open wounds.
